title: Maybe, Never
setting: a cemetery gatekeeper's tally of mourners

post.author: u/night_gate_ottwell
post.title: I keep the night gate at a city cemetery. Three little machines keep our tallies, and this week each of them wrote down something that cannot be true.

blocks.text: Vellmouth General Cemetery has 48,000 graves and one night gatekeeper: me. The gates lock at 19:00. Three small machines keep the tallies, each on a battery and none on any network, because the trust wanted them cheap and the old wall has no cable.

The kiosk stands outside the gate and answers one question: is this person buried here? Its manual says it doesn't keep the names. It keeps a filter of 524,288 bits, tiny switches that are either on or off, and each name in the register switched on 3 of them, each picked by its own hash. If all 3 of a name's switches are on, it answers *may rest here*.

By day every visitor scans a numbered pass at the turnstile. The gate counter there counts the year's different passes in 1,024 one-byte slots its manual calls registers. The turnstile also asks which grave you have come for and adds the visit to the board in my lodge: the year's most visited graves. The board's memory is 3 rows of 256 cells. And Ismay Strade, on the day gate, writes every visitor in the gate book by hand: pass number and grave.
On 9 January, at two in the morning, the kiosk lit up. Through the lodge window I saw a woman in a grey coat typing. Its log:

02:00:14  query   CORISANDE FARRANT
02:00:14  answer  MAY REST HERE

When I got outside with the lantern the screen was still glowing and the path was empty. At 07:30 Phineas Coker, our registrar, went through the register twice. No Corisande Farrant has ever been buried here.
By nine the clerks had finished counting last year's gate book: 14,667 different passes. The gate counter says 14,963. That is 296 mourners nobody wrote down.
And the board says the fourth most visited grave in Vellmouth is number 22,540.
Grave 22,540 is Edwige Danquart, buried 1911. Ivy has covered her name for as long as I've worked here. In last year's gate book nobody visited her once. The board says 1,856 times.

On Friday the trust decides whether to keep the kiosk, print the counter's number in the annual report, and give the restoration money to the board's ten most visited graves first. The day staff won't walk past 22,540 any more. What do I tell them?

blocks.label: three_tallies_9_january.png

diagram.aria: Three machines against three records on 9 January. The kiosk answered may rest here for Corisande Farrant at 02:00; the register, checked at 07:30, has never held her. The gate counter says 14,963 different passes for last year; the gate book says 14,667, 296 fewer. The board puts grave 22,540 fourth with 1,856 visits; the gate book has 0 visits for Edwige Danquart, buried 1911.

blocks.caption: Three machines, three records, one morning. The kiosk said may rest here for a name the register has never held. The gate counter says 14,963 different passes; the gate book, counted by hand, says 14,667. The board puts grave 22,540 fourth with 1,856 visits; the gate book has none.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Your three machines have names. The kiosk is a Bloom filter: a long line of bits where each name switches on a few, picked by hashes; if all of a name's bits are on it says maybe, if any is off it says no. A maybe for a name that was never added is a false positive. The gate counter is a HyperLogLog, which estimates how many different items it has seen in a fixed, small memory; its expected miss either way is its standard error, about 1.04 divided by the square root of the number of registers. The board is a count-min sketch: each visit adds 1 to one cell in every row, and a grave's number is the smallest of its cells. Now some questions. Can your kiosk ever say no to someone who is buried there? Work out the counter's standard error from its manual and put 296 next to it. Which graves share Edwige's three cells? And on Friday, which of the three numbers will be used for what?

replies.author: u/night_gate_ottwell
replies.text: Phineas found the manuals. The kiosk's says a no is always right and a maybe is right most of the time; it gives no figure. The counter's chip has 4 KiB for its tally and the registers use one byte each. The board's says it never shows less than the true count. Ismay's gate book has the grave beside every pass number, so the clerks could count any grave exactly; last year's distinct passes took them the first week of January. Pass numbers are nine digits, printed by the city.

comments.author: u/exact_count_brodie
comments.text: A counter that's 2 percent off is a broken counter. Counting is the one thing a computer can't get wrong: you see a pass, you check whether you've seen it, you add one. Somebody sold your trust a cheap guess. Make it keep every pass number it scans in a list, and the count is exact, the 296 ghosts disappear, and nobody prints a made-up number in an annual report.

comments.author: u/more_bits_sunniva
comments.text: The kiosk is the one that frightens the visitors, so fix that first. These filters get wrong less and less often as you give them more bits; double it three times and the wrong maybes become so rare nobody alive will see one. Memory is cheap. Buy the bigger kiosk and it simply stops saying may rest here for strangers.

reply.prompt: The trust meets on Friday. What should Ottwell tell them to do with the three tallies? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Use each where its error is harmless: kiosk says ask the office, report shows its error, money waits for exact counts.
options.part2: The trust voted on Friday. Phineas changed the kiosk's words: on a maybe it now says 'perhaps: ask at the office in the morning', and on a no, 'not in our register'. In February a man typed a name at 03:10 and got perhaps; by nine Phineas had found her in the register, buried 1964. The annual report printed '14,963 different passes, give or take 486', with a line on how the counter works. For the money, the clerks counted only the board's top 20 graves in the gate book, 20 instead of 48,000. Grave 22,540 had 0 visits and was dropped; all ten of the truly most visited graves were on the shortlist, and they got the money. Nobody has typed Corisande Farrant again. Ismay cut the ivy back from Edwige Danquart's name anyway.
options.senior: Each machine has one kind of error, and the fix is to put it where that error is cheap. A Bloom filter's maybe should lead to a cheap check, while its no can be trusted. An estimate should be printed with its error. And nothing gets paid on a sketch: use it to shortlist, then count the shortlist exactly. Count-min never under-counts, so a grave that is truly popular stays high on the board; in this year's visits the top 20 held all of the true top 10.

options.text: Fit the kiosk with a filter so large it never again says 'may rest here' for anyone who is not buried in our ground.
options.part2: The trust bought a kiosk with 512 KiB, eight times the bits. Corisande Farrant now gets 'not in our register'. The maker's sheet says about 1 stranger in 26,000 still gets may rest here, and in their test of 20,000 made-up names, 1 did. 'So not never,' said Phineas. 'No size is never,' said the maker. And on a maybe the kiosk still words it like a yes. Meanwhile the annual report printed 14,963 as if it were exact, and the first restoration money went to grave 22,540, still fourth on the board. The ivy was cleared for nobody.
options.senior: A bigger filter makes false positives rarer, roughly (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k, but never zero, and each halving of the rate costs more memory than the last. It also only touches the kiosk: the report and the board keep their own kinds of error. Change what the kiosk says on a maybe rather than chasing a filter that never says one.

options.text: Have the gate counter keep every pass number it scans in a list, so the yearly count is exact and the 2 percent is gone.
options.verdict: Exact count, full in a week
options.part2: The counter was reprogrammed to keep every pass number in a list. Its chip holds 4 KiB: 1,024 nine-digit numbers at 4 bytes each. It was full on 7 January. Last year's list would have needed 58,668 bytes, and the trust ordered a bigger chip for the spring. Even with it, the board still put grave 22,540 fourth with 1,856, because a list of passes says nothing about graves, and the restoration money went to her first. The kiosk still said may rest here for strangers.
options.senior: Counting distinct items exactly needs memory that grows with the number of items: 4 bytes for each of 14,667 passes here, against 1,024 bytes for the counter. And 2.02 percent is inside the counter's standard error of 3.25 percent, so it was never broken. Exact passes also do nothing for the board, whose error comes from shared cells.

options.text: Unplug all three devices and go back to counting by hand at the gate: slower, but every number in the gate book is exact.
options.verdict: Trade-off: exact, and dark at night
options.part2: The trust unplugged all three. The gate book kept every count exact: 14,667 passes, and 0 visits for grave 22,540. But the kiosk was dark, and after 19:00 nobody answered the people at the gate; twice in February Ottwell found a note pushed under the lodge door asking whether someone was buried here. The clerks spent weeks tallying 58,400 visits by grave before the money could be shared. It went to the right graves, in May.
options.senior: Exact counting is right when the data is small, or when money or a legal record depends on it, and it is slow and needs people. Here it gives correct money and no answers at night. The machines were fine at what they are for; what was missing was a rule for when to check them.

sim.title: Run Vellmouth's three tallies
sim.lede: You're Ottwell at 01:59 on 9 January, with last year in the three machines. The kiosk's filter holds the register's 48,000 names, one per grave, with a number of hashes per name you can change, and it is also tested on 20,000 made-up names that are not in the register. The gate counter has 1,024 registers and has seen last year's 58,400 visits, 160 a day, drawn from 15,000 regular visitors with nine-digit passes; the gate book has the exact count. The board has 3 rows of 256 cells and shows its top 10 beside the gate book. All three use one hash function, each with its own starting number, picked so that last year comes out as the post tells it. Next entry walks the night: the kiosk at 02:00, the register at 07:30, the gate book at 09:00, the board at 10:15. Change the sizes, the visits (last year, or January to March only) and how the trust uses the tallies, and read each answer against the exact one and its error bound.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Next entry four times. Corisande Farrant gets may rest here while 263 of 20,000 strangers get maybe (formula 1.385%); the counter says 14,963 against 14,667, +2.02% with a standard error of 3.25%; grave 22,540 shows 1,856 with 0 visits, 4th. Set 7 hashes: Corisande clears, 107 of 20,000 still get maybe. Set 512 KiB: 1 still does. Try 16 registers (11,909) and 4,096 (14,904). Widen the board to 512 cells: grave 22,540 drops to 82, off the board. Then try each plan: count the top 20 exactly and grave 22,540 is dropped; keep every pass number and 4 KiB is full on 7 January; count by hand and nobody answers at 02:00.

explain.oneLine: Nothing walked the paths. Each machine did exactly what its design promises: the kiosk's Bloom filter said maybe for a name it never held, the counter's HyperLogLog is 2.02 percent over, inside its 3.25 percent standard error, and the board's count-min sketch over-counted a grave that shares a cell with a busy grave in every row.

steps.title: The kiosk: maybe, or certainly not.
steps.text: A Bloom filter keeps no names. Adding a name switches on k bits chosen by k hashes; asking about a name checks those k bits. If any is off, the name was never added: a no is always right, and the sim's kiosk says no to 0 of its 48,000 names. If all are on, the name may have been added, or other names may have switched those bits on between them. That maybe for a stranger is a false positive. Broder and Mitzenmacher's survey gives the rate as roughly (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k for n names in m bits: with 48,000 names, 524,288 bits and 3 hashes it is 1.385 percent, about 1 stranger in 72, and in the sim 263 of 20,000 made-up names got maybe. Corisande Farrant's three bits had all been switched on by other people's names. A plain Bloom filter can't delete a name either: switching its bits off would switch off bits that other names share.

steps.title: The gate counter: how many, give or take.
steps.text: HyperLogLog counts different items without remembering them. It hashes each pass number; the first 10 bits of the hash pick one of 1,024 registers, and the register keeps the longest run of leading zeros it has seen in the rest. A long run is rare, so it hints at many different passes, and a pass seen twice changes nothing, which is why it counts distinct items. The counter combines all 1,024 registers into one estimate. Flajolet and colleagues give its standard error as about 1.04 divided by the square root of the number of registers: 1.04 / 32 = 3.25 percent, about 486 on 14,963. The counter is 296 over, 2.02 percent: less than one standard error. It uses 1,024 bytes; a list of every pass would need 58,668. Below about 2.5 times its registers, 2,560 here, the estimate needs a small-range correction; 14,667 is far above that.

steps.title: The board: never under, sometimes far over.
steps.text: A count-min sketch keeps d rows of w cells. Each visit adds 1 to one cell per row, chosen by that row's hash, and a grave's number is the smallest of its d cells. Other graves can only add to a cell, so the number is never below the truth: in the sim, 0 of 48,000 graves show less than the gate book. Cormode and Muthukrishnan prove it is over by at most (e / w) times the total, with probability at least 1 - e^(-d). For 256 cells, 3 rows and 58,400 visits: at most 620 over, with probability at least 95 percent. Edwige Danquart's three cells are shared with grave 2,290 (2,602 visits), grave 18,802 (1,705) and grave 7,316 (3,513); the smallest cell holds 1,856, so the board shows 1,856. She is one of 3 graves out of 48,000 that land outside the 95 percent. With 512 cells per row she shows 82 and drops off the board.

steps.title: When exact is better.
steps.text: These structures earn their place when the data is huge, memory is small and an answer that is roughly right is useful. Exact is better when the data is small (the office's register of 48,000 names fits on any office computer), when money changes hands, and when the record is legal or official. The usual pattern combines them: the sketch makes a shortlist cheaply, and an exact count decides. Counting the board's top 20 in the gate book is 20 counts, not 48,000, and because count-min never under-counts, a truly busy grave rarely falls below the shortlist; in last year's visits the top 20 held all of the true top 10. One more exception: if the items were small, dense numbers, a bitmap with one bit per possible number would count them exactly in little memory. Nine-digit passes would need 900 million bits.

diagram.aria: The fix. The kiosk's maybe sends the visitor to the office register in the morning, and its no stands. The gate counter's 14,963 goes into the annual report with plus or minus 486. The board's top 20 becomes a shortlist that the clerks count exactly in the gate book; grave 22,540 has 0 and is dropped, and the restoration money goes to the true top 10.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for next year. Each machine answers only what its error allows: the kiosk's maybe becomes a walk to the office, the counter's number goes into the report with its error, and the board only makes a shortlist that the gate book counts exactly before any money moves.

fix.title: The fix: let each tally answer only what its error allows
fix.text: Keep all three machines and change what each answer is allowed to do. The kiosk says 'perhaps: ask at the office in the morning' on a maybe and 'not in our register' on a no, because a no is always right and a maybe is wrong about 1 time in 72. The annual report prints '14,963 different passes, give or take 486' and says the number is an estimate. The board stays on the lodge wall but pays nobody: each January the clerks count its top 20 graves exactly in the gate book, and the money follows those exact counts. In the sim, that drops grave 22,540, with 0 visits, and every one of the true top 10 is on the shortlist.

limits: A maybe still sends some people to the office for nothing, about 1 stranger in 72 at these settings, and a no is only as good as the register behind the filter: a misspelled or missing entry gets a confident no.

The shortlist works because count-min only over-counts, but enough phantom graves could push a truly busy one below 20. Last year's top 20 held the whole true top 10; check the margin again each year rather than assuming it.

Give or take 486 is one standard error: on most streams the true count falls inside it roughly two times in three, not always. A report that needs a firmer promise should print a wider range, or the exact count.

explain.seniorTake: Probabilistic structures trade a known, bounded error for a fixed, small memory, and each has its own kind of error. A Bloom filter can say maybe wrongly but never no wrongly; HyperLogLog is off by a percentage either way, set by its memory; count-min only ever over-counts. Before using one, ask what its mistake costs. Where the cost is a cheap second check, a line of context, or a slightly wrong chart, use it freely and say how wrong it can be. Where money, billing or a legal record depends on the answer, use it to narrow the search and let an exact count decide. And when the data is small, skip the cleverness and count.

realWorld.title: Bloom, 1970: hash coding with allowable errors
realWorld.text: Burton Bloom's paper in Communications of the ACM, 'Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors', introduced the idea. Broder and Mitzenmacher's survey says Bloom introduced Bloom filters in the 1970s, and that ever since they have been very popular in database applications.

realWorld.title: The Bloom filter principle, and its rate
realWorld.text: Broder and Mitzenmacher state it this way: wherever a list or set is used, and space is at a premium, consider using a Bloom filter if the effect of false positives can be mitigated. Their survey gives the false positive rate as approximately (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k, and explains why a plain filter can't delete: setting a deleted element's bits to 0 may clear a location that another element in the set hashes to. Counting Bloom filters, with small counters instead of bits, were introduced for that.

realWorld.title: HyperLogLog, 2007: about 1.04 / sqrt(m)
realWorld.text: Flajolet, Fusy, Gandouet and Meunier, 'HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm', say the relative accuracy (the standard error) is typically about 1.04/sqrt(m) for m memory units, and that it makes it possible to estimate cardinalities well beyond 10^9 with a typical accuracy of 2% while using a memory of only 1.5 kilobytes.

realWorld.title: HyperLogLog's small-range correction
realWorld.text: The paper's program checks whether the raw estimate is at most 5/2 m; if so, and some registers are still 0, it uses m log(m/V), where V is the number of registers equal to 0. Above that range the raw estimate is used. Vellmouth's 14,667 passes are far above 2,560, so the plain estimate applies.

realWorld.title: Count-min sketch, 2005: never under, rarely far over
realWorld.text: Cormode and Muthukrishnan's 'An Improved Data Stream Summary: The Count-Min Sketch and its Applications' appeared in the Journal of Algorithms in 2005. Its abstract introduces the Count-Min Sketch as a new sublinear space data structure for summarizing data streams, answering point, range and inner product queries approximately and finding frequent items and quantiles.

realWorld.title: Count-min's guarantee: Theorem 1
realWorld.text: The paper's 2004 conference version sets the width to ceil(e/epsilon) and the depth to ceil(ln 1/delta). Its Theorem 1 says the estimate is at least the true count and, with probability at least 1 - delta, at most the true count plus epsilon times the total of all counts. It names the sketch after its two basic operations: counting first and computing the minimum next.

realWorld.title: Redis HyperLogLog: 12 KB, 0.81 percent
realWorld.text: The Redis docs say: 'The Redis implementation uses up to 12 KB of memory and provides a standard error rate of 0.81%.' You add items with PFADD, read the estimate with PFCOUNT and combine two with PFMERGE. 0.81 percent is what 1.04 / sqrt(m) gives for 16,384 registers.

realWorld.title: Redis Bloom filters: guaranteed absence
realWorld.text: The Redis docs say a Bloom filter 'can guarantee the absence of an item from a set, but it can only give an estimation about its presence.' They size it from the error rate: a 1% error rate requires 7 hash functions and 9.585 bits per item.

realWorld.title: Redis count-min sketch: the phantom, described
realWorld.text: The Redis docs describe the probability setting as the chance of an element that has a count below the threshold to collide with elements that had a count above the threshold on all sketches/depths, thus returning a min-count of a frequently occurring element instead of its own. They add that very low counts should be ignored as noise.

realWorld.title: Cassandra: a Bloom filter for each data file
realWorld.text: Apache Cassandra keeps a Bloom filter for each SSTable, built when the file is written. A false positive means Cassandra may scan an SSTable for a row only to find that it does not exist. The bloom_filter_fp_chance setting defaults to 0.01, or 0.1 for tables using LeveledCompactionStrategy, and lower chances use more memory.

asked: How would you count unique visitors to a site with billions of hits?
What is a Bloom filter, and where would you use one?
How do you find the top items in a stream without storing every item?
interview.answer: Start by asking whether the answer must be exact. For unique visitors, an exact count needs memory that grows with the number of visitors, so for a dashboard use HyperLogLog: hash each visitor id, keep a fixed set of registers, and read an estimate whose standard error is about 1.04 divided by the square root of the register count; Redis's PFADD and PFCOUNT give about 0.81 percent in up to 12 KB, and sketches merge, so you can keep one per day and combine them. If the number drives billing, count exactly from the raw events. A Bloom filter answers 'is this in the set?' in a small fixed memory: no is always right, yes means maybe, with a false positive rate of roughly (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k. Use it in front of something expensive, such as skipping SSTables that can't hold a key or checking a username before the database, where a false maybe only costs a lookup. Say that a plain one can't delete. For top items in a stream, keep a count-min sketch: d rows of w cells, add one cell per row, read the minimum. It never under-counts and is over by at most (e / w) times the total with probability 1 - e^(-d). Keep a small heap of the current top candidates, then confirm them with exact counts if the result matters, because a rare item can collide with popular ones in every row.

terms.def: The person who keeps the cemetery gate and lodge at night. Not the course's Gatekeeper load balancer: here it's Ottwell's job.
The small house at a cemetery gate where the gatekeeper works. Vellmouth's board hangs on its wall.
The office's book of everyone buried in the cemetery, with each grave's number. Vellmouth's holds 48,000 names, one per grave.
The person who keeps the burial register. At Vellmouth that's Phineas Coker.
Vellmouth's handwritten record of every day visitor: pass number and grave. Exact, but slow to count.
A card with a nine-digit number that each visitor scans at the turnstile. The same visitor scans the same pass each time.
A gate with rotating arms that lets one person through at a time. Vellmouth's reads visitor passes and asks which grave you've come for.
A stand-alone screen for the public. Vellmouth's is offline and answers one question: is this person buried here?
The battery device on Vellmouth's turnstile that counts the year's different visitor passes, with HyperLogLog.
The list on the lodge wall of the year's most visited graves, kept by a count-min sketch.
The body that runs the cemetery and decides how its money is spent, including restoration money for old graves.
Money the trust spends repairing old graves and headstones. Vellmouth's plan: the most visited graves first.
The trust's yearly public account of what it did, including how many visitors came.
Not connected to any network. The three machines can't check the office's records at night.
The smallest piece of computer data: a single switch that is either 0 (off) or 1 (on). Eight bits make a byte.
A structure that answers from a small, fixed memory by accepting a known chance or size of error. Bloom filters, HyperLogLog and count-min sketches are the common three.
A row of m bits. Adding an item switches on k bits picked by k hashes; asking checks them. Any off: certainly not added. All on: maybe.
How many bits a Bloom filter switches on for each item, each picked by a different hash. The kiosk uses 3.
A yes for something that isn't there: a Bloom filter's maybe for an item that was never added. The kiosk's answer for Corisande Farrant.
A no for something that is there. A plain Bloom filter never gives one, unless someone switches bits off.
How often a stranger gets a maybe: roughly (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k for n items in m bits with k hashes. 1.385% for the kiosk.
A mathematical constant, about 2.718, that appears in growth and probability formulas. e^(-x) means e to the power of minus x.
A Bloom filter with a small counter in each place instead of a bit, so an item can be removed by counting its places down.
The number of different items in a collection. The gate book's cardinality of passes last year: 14,667.
A structure that estimates how many different items it has seen, in a fixed memory of registers, from the longest runs of leading zeros in their hashes.
One small slot of a HyperLogLog. Each keeps the longest run of leading zeros seen among the hashes sent to it. The counter has 1,024.
The 0 bits at the start of a binary number before the first 1. A hash starting with ten zeros turns up about once in 1,024 items.
A number worked out to be close to the true one, not counted exactly. The counter's 14,963 is an estimate.
The typical size of an estimate's miss, either way. For HyperLogLog about 1.04 / sqrt(registers): 3.25% for 1,024.
HyperLogLog's switch, when the raw estimate is at most 2.5 times its registers and some are still 0, to linear counting.
Estimating a small count from how many registers are still empty: m times ln(m / empty registers).
d rows of w counters. Each item adds 1 to one cell per row, picked by that row's hash; its estimate is the smallest of its cells. Never under.
A count-min sketch's counters, laid out as d rows of w cells. Each row has its own hash; many items share each cell.
Two different items landing in the same place, such as the same cell of a sketch's row. Grave 22,540 collides with a busy grave in all 3 rows.
A count-min sketch's cells per row (w) and rows (d). The board is 256 wide and 3 deep: 3,072 bytes at 4 bytes a cell.
A count-min sketch's error and failure chance: w = ceil(e / epsilon), d = ceil(ln(1 / delta)). Over by at most epsilon times the total, except with chance delta.
A stated limit on how wrong an answer can be, often with a probability. The board: at most 620 over, with probability at least 95%.
A small set of candidates picked cheaply, then checked properly. The board's top 20, counted exactly in the gate book.
A count that is correct to the last item, such as the clerks' 14,667 from the gate book. Needs memory or work that grows with the data.
One bit per possible item, on if seen. Exact and tiny when items are small, dense numbers; huge when they are not.
Data that arrives one item at a time, too much or too fast to store whole, such as every visit through a turnstile.
20,000 made-up names that are not in the register, used to measure how often the kiosk says maybe wrongly.
Redis's HyperLogLog commands: add items to a HyperLogLog key, read its estimate of distinct items, and merge several into one.
A sorted, write-once data file on disk in Cassandra and other LSM stores. A read may check several; s3e13 covers them.
A storage engine that collects writes in memory, then writes them out as sorted files on disk that are merged later. Cassandra is one; s3e13 covers it.
Cassandra's per-table setting for its SSTable Bloom filters' false positive chance. Lower uses more memory.
One of Cassandra's ways of merging SSTables on disk. Its tables get a Bloom filter false positive chance of 0.1 by default.
A structure that keeps the largest few items seen so far and quickly drops the smallest. Used with a sketch to track a top-k list.
The number of different people who used a product in a period, each counted once however often they came.

atWork: Look for numbers in your systems that come from a sketch, and ask what their mistakes cost. The common case is a product dashboard that shows 'unique users' from HyperLogLog, such as Redis's PFCOUNT, which is fine for a chart; then finance starts billing customers per unique user from the same number, and a customer's own logs disagree by a fraction of a percent. Nothing is broken, but money now rests on an estimate. The fix is exact counts wherever money is involved, from the raw events or a table of distinct ids, with the sketch kept for the dashboard. Do the same audit for Bloom filters (what happens on a false maybe, and does anything ever try to delete from one?) and for top-k lists from a count-min sketch (does anything pay out, rank people or block traffic on them without an exact check?). Write down each structure's size and its error: m, n and k for a filter, the register count for HyperLogLog, w and d for count-min. One line back to the case before this one: Cassandra and other LSM stores keep a Bloom filter per SSTable, so a read can skip files that can't hold the key (s3e13). If your company is pursuing a SOC 2 report that includes the processing integrity category, its criteria (PI1.3 in the AICPA's 2017 Trust Services Criteria) expect data to be processed completely and accurately; billing from an estimate is the kind of gap an auditor can ask about, so put exact counts behind every billed number from the first design rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your analytics dashboard shows unique users per customer from a HyperLogLog with 16,384 registers, and finance has started billing customers per unique user from that number. A customer's own logs show 50,000 unique users for March; you billed them for 50,400. Is the dashboard broken, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: It isn't broken: 400 on 50,000 is inside HyperLogLog's standard error, about 1.04 divided by the square root of the registers
Bill from an exact count of distinct users, from raw events or a table, not from the estimate
Keep the sketch for the dashboard, and show its number as an estimate with its error

recall.model: It isn't broken. HyperLogLog's standard error is about 1.04 divided by the square root of its registers, 1.04 / 128 = 0.81 percent for 16,384, which is about 400 on 50,000, so 50,400 is exactly the size of miss it was designed to make. The mistake is billing from it. Bill from an exact count of distinct users per customer, from the raw events or a table of user ids, and keep the sketch for the dashboard, where its number is shown as approximate, give or take its error.

recall.prompt: A service keeps a Bloom filter of every username taken. For a new username, the filter says it is not in the set. What can you conclude?
options: The username is certainly not in the set
The username is probably not in the set, about 99 times in 100
The username might be in the set, so check the database
Nothing, until the filter is rebuilt from the database
recall.why: If any of the username's k bits is off, it was never added, so a no is always right. Only a yes is uncertain: all k bits on can mean the name was added, or that other names switched those bits on. That's why a filter's no can skip the database, while a yes needs the real check. A plain filter loses this promise only if someone switches bits off to delete.

recall.prompt: Your app shows 'trending this hour' from a sketch with 4 rows of 2,000 counters: each post adds 1 to one counter per row, and a tag's number is the smallest of its 4. An obscure tag with almost no posts appears in the top 10. Why can that happen, and how would you make sure the trending list is right before it goes out?

keyIdeas.idea: In every row the obscure tag shares a counter with a popular tag, so even its smallest counter is high
A count-min sketch only over-counts, by at most e/w of the total with probability 1 - e^-d, so a high number for a rare item is possible
Use the sketch as a shortlist and confirm the candidates with exact counts (or a wider sketch) before publishing

recall.model: It's a count-min sketch, and in every row the obscure tag shares a counter with a popular tag, so even the smallest of its 4 counters is high: a collision in each row. Count-min never under-counts; it overestimates by at most e/2,000 of the hour's total with probability 1 - e^-4, about 98 percent, so across thousands of tags a few will land far over. Before publishing, treat the sketch's top 30 or so as a shortlist of candidates and count each one exactly from the hour's posts, then rank by the exact counts. If phantoms are common, use a wider sketch: more counters per row shrink the bound.

recall.prompt: A HyperLogLog has 1,024 registers. About what is its standard error?
recall.why: The standard error is about 1.04 divided by the square root of the number of registers: 1.04 / 32 = 3.25 percent. That's why Vellmouth's counter being 2.02 percent off its gate book is normal. Redis's 0.81 percent matches 16,384 registers, and 1.6 percent would be 4,096.

recall.prompt: In a count-min sketch, how can an item's estimate compare with its true count?
options: Higher or lower, about equally often
Always exact once the count passes 100
recall.why: Every cell an item uses holds its own count plus whatever other items added there, so each cell is at least the true count, and so is the smallest. Collisions can only push it up. Cormode and Muthukrishnan bound how far: at most epsilon times the total, with probability at least 1 - delta.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The kiosk says perhaps now, the report printed its range, and the money went by the gate book. Thank you all. But in May the city moved 300 graves from the flooded north corner to a new ground across the river. Phineas asked the kiosk's maker to take the 300 moved names out, and their technician switched off each moved name's 3 switches. Since then the kiosk has said 'not in our register' to at least four families whose people have never left Vellmouth. One of them was Ismay, asking about her mother.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why does the kiosk now say no for people who are buried at Vellmouth, and how should moved names come out of it?

keyIdeas.idea: Names share bits: switching off a moved name's bits also switched off bits other buried names need, so the filter now gives false negatives
A plain Bloom filter can't delete; rebuild it from the current register instead
If names must come out often, use a counting Bloom filter, with counters that go down, or another structure that supports deletes

coldCase.model: Each switch in the filter is shared: the 3 switches a moved name had turned on were also turned on by other names, and some of those names still rest at Vellmouth. Switching them off broke the one promise the filter makes, so now it gives false negatives: a confident no for Ismay's mother. A plain Bloom filter can't delete. To take names out, rebuild the filter from scratch from the current register, which is quick for 48,000 names, and load the new filter into the kiosk. If names had to come out often, a counting Bloom filter, with a small counter in each place that goes down on a delete, would allow it at a few times the memory.

Philippe Flajolet, Eric Fusy, Olivier Gandouet and Frederic Meunier, HyperLogLog: the analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm, AofA 07, DMTCS Proceedings vol. AH, 2007 (standard error typically about 1.04/sqrt(m); cardinalities well beyond 10^9 with a typical accuracy of 2% using 1.5 kilobytes)

Flajolet, Fusy, Gandouet and Meunier, HyperLogLog (full paper PDF: the HYPERLOGLOG program, alpha constants 0.673, 0.697, 0.709 and 0.7213/(1 + 1.079/m), small range correction m log(m/V) when the estimate is at most 5/2 m)
Graham Cormode and S. Muthukrishnan, An Improved Data Stream Summary: The Count-Min Sketch and its Applications, Journal of Algorithms 55(1):58-75, 2005 (citation page)

Cormode and Muthukrishnan, An Improved Data Stream Summary: The Count-Min Sketch and its Applications, LATIN 2004 conference version (w = ceil(e/epsilon), d = ceil(ln 1/delta); Theorem 1: estimate at least the true count and, with probability at least 1 - delta, at most the true count plus epsilon times the total; named after counting first and computing the minimum next)
Redis Docs: HyperLogLog (up to 12 KB of memory and a standard error rate of 0.81%; PFADD, PFCOUNT, PFMERGE)
Redis Docs: Bloom filter (can guarantee the absence of an item but only estimate its presence; 1% error rate requires 7 hash functions and 9.585 bits per item)

Redis Docs: Count-min sketch (over-counting due to collisions; very low counts should be ignored as noise; probability as the chance a low-count element collides with high-count elements on all depths)

Apache Cassandra Documentation (stable): Bloom filters (one per SSTable, persisted as its Filter component; false positives scan an SSTable for a row that does not exist; bloom_filter_fp_chance 0.01 by default, 0.1 for LeveledCompactionStrategy)
